transcript.text: People say you should just burn the
boats and go all in. Is that actually
the right way to take a big risk?
>> I'm a huge fan in play of plan B's, but
I want my plan B to continue to level
up. And so, I remember that when I
started my business, my plan B was that
if this didn't work and I spent all my
savings on my gym, that I knew that I
could drive Uber and strip. And if I
could do that, I'd be able to make
another $150,000 a year, take the extra
cash, and then try you know, try to
start over again. Once I learned how to
sell, that was the first real skill I
learned. I was like, "Okay, well I can
start selling cars and probably make
200, 300, 400,000 a year depending on
what kind of cars I was selling. And I
could do that and hustle really hard for
a year, and then go back out if I really
wanted to. And then once I learned how
to market, I knew that I could make a
million dollars a year because I could
just go get leads and sell them myself
and then ask for a significantly larger
portion of the business. Every risk that
I've had to take in business, the
[music] skill set has basically given me
a backstop to fall back to, knowing that
I can take this bigger swing because my
worst case scenario is still fine. And I
think that knowing that your worst case
is actually not death is what unleashes
you to go take big swings.
